Definition (1 mark)

Hypersensitivity refers to an exaggerated or inappropriate immune response of a previously sensitised host to an otherwise harmless antigen ("allergen"), resulting in tissue injury, inflammation, or dysfunction. The response occurs on re-exposure to the antigen — the first exposure produces sensitisation, subsequent exposures trigger the reaction. Coombs & Gell (1963) classified hypersensitivity into four types (Type V added later).

Classification (Gell & Coombs) (3 marks)

Type Mechanism Onset Examples

Type II — Antibody-dependent cytotoxicIgG/IgM against cell-surface or matrix antigen → complement, opsonisation, ADCCMinutes–hoursBlood transfusion reactions, haemolytic disease of newborn, ITP, Goodpasture, Graves, myasthenia gravis, pemphigus
Type III — Immune-complexAntigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissues → complement → neutrophil recruitment & damage3–10 hoursSerum sickness, SLE, post-streptococcal GN, polyarteritis nodosa, Arthus reaction, farmer's lung

Type V — Stimulatory / anti-receptorIgG binds cell-surface receptor → stimulates (or blocks) signallingVariableGraves disease (anti-TSHR stimulates TSH receptor → hyperthyroid), myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR blocking)

Type I Hypersensitivity — Mechanism (6 marks)

Phase 1 — Sensitisation (first exposure)

  1. Allergen entry — low-dose allergen (pollen, dust mite, food, insect venom, drug) enters via mucosal/skin route.
  2. Antigen presentation — dendritic cells / Langerhans cells capture allergen, process & present peptide on MHC-II to naïve CD4+ T cells in draining lymph node.
  3. Th2 polarisation — in atopic individuals (genetic predisposition — IL-4, IL-13 polymorphisms, high IgE locus on chromosome 5q), naïve CD4+ T cells differentiate into Th2 cells (rather than Th1). This is promoted by IL-4 from basophils & iNKT cells.
  4. Cytokine cascade — Th2 cells secrete:
    • IL-4 → B-cell class switching from IgM to IgE.
    • IL-5 → eosinophil production, activation, and survival.
    • IL-13 → goblet cell hyperplasia, mucus hypersecretion, airway hyper-responsiveness.
    • IL-9 → mast cell proliferation.
    • IL-25, IL-33, TSLP — epithelium-derived alarmins amplify Th2.
  5. IgE production & mast cell sensitisation — B cells mature into plasma cells secreting allergen-specific IgE. IgE binds the high-affinity FcεRI receptor on mast cells (tissue) & basophils (blood); the host is now "sensitised" but asymptomatic. This sensitisation can persist for months–years.

Phase 2 — Effector phase (re-exposure) — Immediate reaction (15–30 min)

  1. Allergen cross-linking — re-exposed allergen binds & cross-links two adjacent FcεRI-bound IgE molecules on the mast cell surface.
  2. Signal transduction — Lyn & Syk kinases phosphorylate ITAMs → PLCγ → IP3 + DAG → Ca²⁺ release & PKC activation → degranulation.
  3. Mast cell degranulation — three waves of mediators:
    • Preformed (primary) mediators — released from granules within seconds: histamine (vasodilation, ↑permeability, bronchoconstriction, mucus, itch), tryptase, chymase, heparin, serotonin (rodents), eosinophil chemotactic factor-A (ECF-A), neutrophil chemotactic factor (NCF-A), proteases.
    • Lipid-derived (secondary) mediators — generated from arachidonic acid via COX & LOX within minutes: prostaglandin D2 (bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, mucus), leukotrienes C4, D4, E4 (slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis — 100–1000× more potent bronchoconstrictor than histamine; ↑permeability), LTB4 (neutrophil chemotaxis), platelet-activating factor (platelet aggregation, bronchoconstriction, ↑permeability).
    • Cytokines (tertiary mediators) — synthesised & released over hours: IL-4, IL-13 (amplify Th2/IgE), IL-5 (eosinophils), IL-6, TNF-α (systemic inflammation, fever, endothelial activation), GM-CSF.
  4. Clinical effects — vasodilation & increased vascular permeability (urticaria, angioedema, hypotension), bronchoconstriction (wheeze), mucus hypersecretion (rhinorrhoea), visceral smooth muscle spasm (cramping, diarrhoea, vomiting), sensory nerve stimulation (itch, sneeze).

Phase 3 — Late-phase reaction (LPR, 4–8 hours, persists 24 h)

Driven by secondary mediators & cytokines: leukotrienes, PAF, cytokines recruit eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, and Th2 cells to the site → sustained inflammation, tissue oedema, bronchial hyper-reactivity. This is the pathophysiological basis of the "late asthmatic response" — a second drop in FEV1 at 4–8 h after allergen exposure. Repeated episodes lead to airway remodelling (subepithelial fibrosis, goblet cell metaplasia, smooth muscle hypertrophy).

Diagnosis

  • Skin prick test — allergen applied to skin, prick; wheal & flare within 15–20 min (Type I).
  • Intradermal test — more sensitive, less specific; used for venom & drug allergy.
  • Serum allergen-specific IgE (RAST/ImmunoCAP) — useful when skin test contraindicated (dermographism, antihistamine use, severe eczema).
  • Total serum IgE — supports atopy but non-specific.
  • Serum tryptase — elevated for ~6 h after anaphylaxis (mast cell activation marker).
  • Oral food challenge / bronchial provocation — gold standard but specialist-only.
  • Patch test — for Type IV (allergic contact dermatitis), read at 48–72 h.

Management Principles

  • Allergen avoidance — primary measure.
  • Antihistamines (H1 blockers — cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) — block histamine effects; more effective for rhinitis/urticaria than asthma.
  • Mast cell stabilisers — cromolyn sodium, nedocromil.
  • Leukotriene receptor antagonists — montelukast, zafirlukast (block LTD4 receptor).
  • β2-agonists (salbutamol) — bronchodilation; inhaled corticosteroids for chronic asthma.
  • Glucocorticoids — topical (eczema, rhinitis), inhaled (asthma), systemic (severe exacerbations).
  • Adrenaline (epinephrine) — IM 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) — first-line for anaphylaxis; α-agonist vasoconstriction, β1 increases cardiac output, β2 bronchodilates, stabilises mast cells.
  • Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody — omalizumab (binds free IgE, downregulates FcεRI) for severe allergic asthma & chronic urticaria.
  • Allergen immunotherapy (desensitisation) — subcutaneous or sublingual, gradually increasing allergen dose → IgG4 (blocking antibody) production, Treg induction, Th2 → Th1 shift. Effective for venom, pollen, dust mite allergy.
  • Biologics — mepolizumab, benralizumab (anti-IL-5) for eosinophilic asthma; dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) for asthma & atopic dermatitis.

Atopy

Atopy is the genetic predisposition to develop IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to common environmental allergens. Atopic individuals have high baseline IgE, positive skin tests to multiple allergens, eosinophilia, and a family history of atopy ("atopic triad" — asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis). Atopy accounts for ~40–50% of the genetic risk; environmental factors (hygiene hypothesis — reduced microbial exposure in early life skews immune response toward Th2) contribute the rest.

Clinical Pearl

The double-wave response — immediate (15–30 min, mast-cell histamine) followed by late-phase (4–8 h, eosinophil-driven via cytokines & leukotrienes) — is the hallmark of Type I hypersensitivity and explains why bronchodilators alone (treating the immediate wave) are insufficient. Inhaled corticosteroids target the late phase and airway remodelling; this is the rationale for combined ICS/LABA therapy (e.g., budesonide/formoterol) as step 3+ in asthma management. In acute anaphylaxis, adrenaline is the only life-saving drug — antihistamines are adjunctive; never delay adrenaline for any reason. All patients with history of anaphylaxis should carry an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) and wear medical alert identification.

Definitions (2 marks)

  • Sterilization — the complete destruction or removal of all viable microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, spores, and prions (where relevant). A sterile object is free of all microbial life forms.
  • Disinfection — the destruction of pathogenic microorganisms (vegetative bacteria, most viruses, fungi) but not necessarily bacterial spores. Does not produce a sterile object.
  • Antisepsis — disinfection applied to living tissue (skin, mucous membranes) using milder chemicals (antiseptics) — e.g., chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine.
  • Decontamination — removal of pathogenic microorganisms from objects so they are safe to handle (without necessarily sterilising).
  • -cidal vs -static: bactericidal (kills), bacteriostatic (inhibits growth); sporocidal, virucidal, fungicidal, tuberculocidal.

Levels of Disinfection

  • High-level disinfection (HLD) — destroys all vegetative organisms, mycobacteria, viruses, fungi, and some bacterial spores (with prolonged exposure). Used for semi-critical items (endoscopes, respiratory therapy equipment). Agents: glutaraldehyde 2%, ortho-phthalaldehyde, hydrogen peroxide 7.5%, peracetic acid.
  • Intermediate-level disinfection — destroys vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, most viruses & fungi; not spores. Used for non-critical items touched by intact skin (stethoscopes, blood pressure cuffs). Agents: 70% isopropyl alcohol, sodium hypochlorite 1:50, phenolics, iodophors.
  • Low-level disinfection — destroys vegetative bacteria, lipid/enveloped viruses, some fungi; not mycobacteria, spores, or non-enveloped viruses. Agents: quaternary ammonium compounds, 70% alcohol.

Spaulding Classification (clinical relevance)

Category Definition Required Processing Examples
CriticalEnters sterile tissue or vascular systemSterilizationSurgical instruments, implants, cardiac catheters, needles, laparoscopes
Semi-criticalContacts mucous membranes or non-intact skinHigh-level disinfectionEndoscopes, respiratory therapy equipment, laryngoscope blades, vaginal specula
Non-criticalContacts intact skin onlyLow/intermediate disinfectionStethoscopes, BP cuffs, bedpans, surfaces, furniture

Methods of Sterilization (brief overview) (2 marks)

Physical Chemical
  • Heat
    • Moist heat — autoclave (121 °C × 15 min), boiling (100 °C), tyndallisation (fractional, 100 °C × 30 min × 3 days), pasteurisation (63 °C × 30 min / 72 °C × 15 sec).
    • Dry heat — hot air oven (160 °C × 2 h), flaming, incineration.
  • Filtration — membrane (0.22 µm for bacteria), HEPA (air), depth filters; for heat-labile fluids (antibiotics, sera, vaccines).
  • Radiation — ionising (gamma, X-ray — for plastics, sutures, syringes, catheters); non-ionising (UV — surfaces, air in OTs).
  • Sonication / ultrasonic — for delicate instruments.
  • Aldehydes — glutaraldehyde 2%, formaldehyde 37% (formalin 10%), ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA).
  • Oxidising agents — hydrogen peroxide (6–7.5% solution, vapour-phase), peracetic acid, ozone.
  • Halogens — sodium hypochlorite, iodophors (povidone-iodine).
  • Alcohols — 70% ethanol / isopropanol.
  • Phenolics — phenol, carbolic acid, lysol.
  • Quaternary ammonium compounds — benzalkonium chloride, cetrimide.
  • Heavy metals — silver sulfadiazine, mercurochrome (obsolete).
  • Gases — ethylene oxide (EtO), formaldehyde vapour, β-propiolactone, plasma (H₂O₂ vapour-phase).

Moist Heat Sterilizers (enumeration) (2 marks)

  1. Autoclave — saturated steam under pressure (most widely used; 121 °C / 15 psi / 15 min, or 134 °C / 30 psi / 3 min for prion-sensitive instruments).
  2. Boiling water (100 °C × 10–30 min) — disinfection only; spores survive.
  3. Tyndallisation / fractional sterilisation — three successive days of boiling at 100 °C × 30 min; spores germinate between sessions and are killed the next day; for heat-labile fluids (egg, serum, sugar media).
  4. Pasteurisation
    • Holder method — 63 °C × 30 min.
    • Flash (HTST) — 72 °C × 15 sec.
    • Ultra-high temperature (UHT) — 132 °C × 1 sec.
    Used for milk, juices; kills vegetative pathogens (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Coxiella burnetii, Salmonella, Brucella) but not spores.
  5. Steam under pressure — instrument washer-disinfectors (thermal disinfection at 90 °C for M. tuberculosis).
  6. Koch steamer / Arnold steamer — older non-pressurised steam sterilizer (100 °C).

Autoclave — Principle (3 marks)

When water boils in a closed vessel under pressure, the boiling point rises above 100 °C. The autoclave uses saturated steam under pressure (typically 15 psi / 103 kPa above atmospheric pressure) to achieve 121 °C, which is sufficient to kill all microorganisms including bacterial spores within 15 minutes. Sterilisation is achieved by the latent heat of vaporisation released when steam condenses on the cooler surface of the load — rapidly transferring energy and raising the surface temperature to 121 °C. Air is the enemy — air pockets insulate and reduce steam penetration, so it must be displaced either by gravity displacement (downward) or by vacuum-assisted pre-vacuum cycles.

Standard cycles:

  • 121 °C, 15 psi, 15 min — general purpose (wrapped instruments, surgical packs, microbiological media, infectious waste).
  • 134 °C, 30 psi, 3 min — prion-inactivation cycle (BSE/vCJD); used for neurosurgical instruments that have contacted high-risk tissue.
  • 115 °C, 10 psi, 30 min — heat-labile media (sugars, antibiotics).

Autoclave — Construction & Procedure (2 marks)

  1. Chamber — sturdy steel pressure vessel with locking door, safety valve, pressure gauge, temperature gauge, steam inlet, air & condensate outlet.
  2. Steam generator — external or integral; produces saturated steam.
  3. Vacuum pump — in pre-vacuum autoclaves, removes air before steam entry (better penetration).
  4. Drain / condensate trap — removes condensed water.
  5. Procedure:
    1. Load the chamber — packages loosely arranged to allow steam circulation (do not stack tightly; place on racks; standing upright if possible).
    2. Close & lock the door.
    3. Select cycle (gravity or vacuum; 121 °C/15 min or 134 °C/3 min).
    4. Air is removed (gravity displacement or vacuum); steam enters until desired pressure (15 psi) & temperature (121 °C) reached.
    5. Holding time starts when load temperature reaches 121 °C (not chamber temp).
    6. After hold, depressurisation & drying phase (vacuum-assisted for wrapped items).
    7. Unload only when load is dry & cool.

Uses of Autoclave

  • Surgical instruments, linen, gowns, drapes, gloves.
  • Microbiological culture media (nutrient agar, Robertson's cooked meat, Löffler serum — only short cycle).
  • Glassware, laboratory plastics (PP, PMP, PTFE).
  • Biohazardous waste (used cultures, swabs, contaminated material).
  • Aqueous solutions, distilled water, saline.
  • Soiled linen from infectious patients.
  • Items that cannot be autoclaved: heat-labile plastics (PE, PS), oils, greases, powders, sharp instruments that may corrode (use dry heat or EtO instead), electronics, optical instruments (endoscopes — use HLD).

Sterilization Control / Monitoring (3 marks)

Sterilisation must be validated by physical, chemical, and biological indicators.

Physical indicators

  • Pressure gauge, temperature gauge, cycle timer — printed record for each load.
  • Door interlock — prevents opening under pressure.

Chemical indicators (process / external & internal)

  • Tape / external indicator (Bowie-Dick tape) — autoclave tape with diagonal stripes that change colour (cream → black) when exposed to 121 °C. Verifies that the package has been processed — not sterility.
  • Bowie-Dick test — daily test of pre-vacuum autoclave air removal. Special pack with chemical indicator sheet — uniform colour change confirms adequate air removal; spots indicate air pockets → vacuum pump fault.
  • Class 4–6 internal chemical indicators — multi-parameter strips placed inside each package; respond to temperature, time, and steam quality (Class 6 = emulating indicator, equivalent to biological indicator).
  • Vaporised hydrogen peroxide / EtO chemical indicators for low-temperature sterilisers.

Biological indicators (gold standard)

Sterilizer Test organism Reading
Autoclave (moist heat, 121 °C)Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores (10⁶)24–48 h incubation at 55–60 °C; no growth = pass
Hot air oven (dry heat, 160 °C)Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly B. subtilis var. niger) sporesIncubation at 37 °C; no growth = pass
Ethylene oxideBacillus atrophaeus sporesIncubation at 37 °C; no growth = pass
Ionising radiationBacillus pumilus sporesIncubation at 37 °C; no growth = pass

Run biological indicator weekly (or per ISO 11140 recommendation daily for implant loads; for every load containing implants). Self-contained rapid readout biological indicators (incubated in 1–3 h using fluorescent enzyme detection) are now standard.

Clinical Pearl

Always remember: time starts when the load (not the chamber) reaches 121 °C — that is why large or dense loads (e.g., a 5-L flask of liquid) need extended cycles (30–60 min), while a single wrapped instrument may pass in 4 min at 134 °C. Prions (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease) are exceptionally resistant — the WHO recommends 134 °C × 18 min (single vacuum cycle) or 6 cycles of 3 min each, preceded by NaOH 1N soaking for 1 hour, for neurosurgical instruments exposed to high-risk tissue (brain, spinal cord, eye, pituitary). Single-use instruments are preferred for known CJD patients. Also remember the "5 s rule": never assume a sterility indicator in a flat package on the chamber floor represents the most difficult-to-sterilise location — always place indicators in the centre of densest load.

(A) Identification of the Etiological Agent (2 marks)

The clinical picture — persistent diarrhoea, significant weight loss, mild fever in a young adult with a history of unsafe sexual practices with multiple partners — is highly suggestive of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) with HIV-wasting syndrome and possibly opportunistic infection (e.g., cryptosporidiosis, Isospora, microsporidiosis, CMV colitis).

The causative agent is the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) — most likely HIV-1 (responsible for the global pandemic; >95% of cases in India). HIV-2 is largely confined to West Africa, with lower transmissibility and slower disease progression.

Taxonomy: family Retroviridae, subfamily Lentivirinae, genus Lentivirus. Enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded, diploid RNA virus. Contains reverse transcriptase (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase), integrase, and protease enzymes.

Structure: icosahedral capsid (p24) containing two copies of RNA + RT, integrase, protease; surrounded by matrix protein (p17) and lipid bilayer envelope studded with gp120 (surface) and gp41 (transmembrane) glycoproteins derived from the env gene.

Brief Virology & Pathogenesis (context)

  • Receptor & co-receptors — gp120 binds CD4 on T-helper cells, monocytes/macrophages, dendritic cells, microglia; co-receptor is CCR5 (M-tropic/R5 strains — early infection, transmitted) or CXCR4 (T-tropic/X4 strains — late). Individuals homozygous for CCR5-Δ32 mutation are resistant to HIV.
  • Replication — binding → fusion (gp41) → entry → uncoating → reverse transcription (RNA→DNA) → integration into host genome by integrase → proviral DNA → transcription & translation → assembly & budding → maturation by protease.
  • Loss of CD4+ T cells — direct viral cytopathic effect, apoptosis, syncytium formation, CTL-mediated killing; progressive immunodeficiency.
  • Subtypes (clades) — HIV-1 group M (major) has clades A–K; clade C dominant in India & southern Africa. Circulating recombinant forms (CRFs) common.

(B) Laboratory Diagnosis of HIV/AIDS (7 marks)

1. Screening Tests — Antibody Detection (initial assay)

Strategy follows the NACO/WHO serial testing algorithm — three different antigen preparations; sample positive in all three = positive. Window period for antibody-based tests is 3–12 weeks (4th-generation Ag/Ab combination tests reduce to ~2–4 weeks).

Generation Detects Window Method
1stIgG to HIV-1 (viral lysate)6–12 weeksELISA
2ndIgG to HIV-1 & HIV-2 (recombinant/petide antigens)4–6 weeksELISA, rapid tests
3rdIgG + IgM to HIV-1/2 (including group O)3–4 weeksELISA, rapid, CLIA
4thp24 antigen + IgG/IgM antibody2–4 weeksELISA combo (ARCHITECT, VITROS)
5thp24 Ag + HIV-1 Ab + HIV-2 Ab separately reported2–3 weeksCLIA (Abbott)

Rapid tests — immunochromatographic / dot-blot / lateral flow (whole blood, plasma, serum, or oral fluid). WHO pre-qualified: OraQuick, Determine HIV-1/2, Tridot, Insti. Result in 15–20 minutes; used at ICTC/PPTCT centres and self-testing.

2. Supplemental / Confirmatory Tests

  • Western blot — gold standard for confirmation; detects antibodies to specific HIV proteins (gp160, gp120, gp41, p31, p24, p17, p55). Positive = bands to ≥2 of p24, gp41, gp120/160.
  • Recombinant immunoblot (RIBA/LiaTek) — line immunoassay using recombinant antigens; differentiates HIV-1 vs HIV-2.
  • HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation ELISA — for confirmation of type.

3. Molecular Tests — Viral Detection

  • HIV-1 RNA viral load (RT-PCR) — quantitative; detects early infection (window period ~10 days); baseline, monitoring therapy response, diagnosis in infants (maternal antibodies confound serology until 18 months). Target <50 copies/mL = suppressed.
  • HIV-1 DNA PCR (qualitative) — detects proviral DNA in PBMCs; preferred for infant diagnosis (sensitivity 95% at 4–6 weeks of age).
  • Nucleic acid-based testing (NAT) — pooled donor screening — reduces window period to ~7 days.
  • Genotypic resistance testing — before initiating ART (transmitted drug resistance) and at treatment failure; detects mutations in RT, protease, integrase genes.

4. Antigen Detection

  • p24 antigen ELISA — appears ~2 weeks post-infection, before antibody; useful in window period, infant diagnosis, stage 4 disease (loss of antibody with advanced disease).
  • p24 can be dissociated from immune complexes (ICD p24) for higher sensitivity.

5. CD4+ T-cell Counting (staging & monitoring)

  • Flow cytometry — CD4 absolute count & CD4/CD8 ratio. Normal adult CD4 = 500–1500 cells/µL.
  • WHO clinical staging:
Stage CD4 Clinical features

3200–349Oral candidiasis, pulmonary TB, chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, recurrent bacterial pneumonia

6. Other Investigations (workup of symptomatic patient)

  • CBC (anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia), ESR.
  • LFT, RFT, blood glucose (baseline before ART — tenofovir, atazanavir).
  • Serology — HBsAg, anti-HCV, syphilis (RPR/VDRL), anti-Toxoplasma IgG, Cryptococcal antigen (serum & CSF if CD4 <100).
  • Tuberculosis — sputum AFB, CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF), chest X-ray; extra-pulmonary TB workup.
  • Stool — routine microscopy, modified acid-fast stain (Cryptosporidium, Isospora, Cyclospora), microsporidium stain (Chromotrope), stool culture.
  • Chest X-ray — PCP (bilateral interstitial infiltrates), TB (cavitation, effusion).
  • Pap smear / HPV — women (cervical dysplasia).

(C) National Strategies for HIV Diagnosis (NACO, India) (6 marks)

India's national response is coordinated by the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP), currently NACP-V (2021–2025). The diagnostic strategy is structured around the cascade of prevention → testing → linkage to care → treatment → viral suppression.

1. ICTC — Integrated Counselling & Testing Centre

The cornerstone of HIV testing in India. Provides:

  • Pre-test counselling — information on HIV, modes of transmission, risk assessment, meaning of test results, consent.
  • HIV testing — using NACO-approved rapid test kits following the serial algorithm:
    1. Test 1 (e.g., Comb AIDS) — if non-reactive, report negative (after window-period counselling).
    2. If reactive → Test 2 with different antigen/kit (e.g., Determine HIV-1/2).
    3. If reactive → Test 3 (tie-breaker, different antigen — e.g., Tridot/Pareekshak).
    4. If all three reactive → report positive.
    5. If discordant (Test 1 +, Test 2 –) → retest after 2–4 weeks; or perform nucleic acid test (NAT).
  • Post-test counselling — for positive: disclosure, partner notification, linkage to ART centre, psychosocial support. For negative: risk reduction, window period, retesting.

2. PPTCT — Prevention of Parent-to-Child Transmission (now "Elimination of Vertical Transmission")

  • Universal HIV screening of all pregnant women at ANC clinics.
  • HIV-positive mothers receive lifelong ART (Option B+) — TDF + 3TC + DTG (Dolutogravir) — to reduce vertical transmission to <2%.
  • Baby receives NVP (Nevirapine) syrup for 6–12 weeks; C-section if maternal viral load high; exclusive replacement feeding (formula) or exclusive breastfeeding (depending on national policy) for 6 months.

3. Early Infant Diagnosis (EID)

  • HIV-1 DNA PCR on dried blood spot (DBS) at 4–6 weeks of age, 6 months, 6 weeks after cessation of breastfeeding, and any symptomatic infant.
  • Positive → immediately start ART; confirm with second DNA PCR.

4. TB-HIV Co-infection

  • All TB patients (newly diagnosed) must be offered HIV testing (routine "provider-initiated HIV testing & counselling — PITC").
  • All HIV-positive patients screened for TB with 4-symptom screen (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss); if positive → CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF).
  • Three I's: Intensified TB case finding, Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT 6 months), Infection control.

5. Targeted Interventions (TI) for High-Risk Groups

  • Female sex workers (FSW), men who have sex with men (MSM), injecting drug users (IDU), transgender people, migrants, truckers.
  • Outreach testing, peer educators, condom promotion, needle-syringe exchange, OST (opioid substitution therapy), STI management, linkage to ART.

6. ART Programme

  • Treat All policy (Test & Treat) since 2017 — every person diagnosed with HIV is offered lifelong ART regardless of CD4 count.
  • First-line ART (NACO 2023): TDF + 3TC + DTG (TLD regimen — Dolutogravir-based).
  • Second-line: TDF + 3TC + ATV/r (Atazanavir/ritonavir) or LPV/r after resistance testing.
  • Third-line: Darunavir/ritonavir + Etravirine + Raltegravir/Dolutegravir.
  • Viral load monitoring — at 6 months, 12 months, then annually; target <1000 copies/mL (treatment failure threshold).

7. Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) & Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)

  • PEP — for occupational (needle-stick) & sexual exposure: TDF + 3TC + DTG for 28 days, started within 72 hours (ideally <2 h).
  • PrEP — daily TDF/FTC for high-risk serodiscordant couples, MSM, FSW; demonstration projects in India.

8. Stigma Reduction & Legal Framework

  • HIV & AIDS (Prevention & Control) Act, 2017 — prohibits discrimination in employment, education, healthcare, insurance; mandates informed consent & confidentiality.

Clinical Pearl

The 4th-generation Ag/Ab ELISA has shortened the diagnostic window to ~2–4 weeks by detecting p24 antigen (which appears before antibody) and is now the recommended first-line screening test globally. (A) Identification & Definition (2 marks)

The clinical picture — redness, swelling, purulent discharge, fever, leucocytosis at the surgical site 5 days after abdominal surgery — is the textbook presentation of a Surgical Site Infection (SSI), a subtype of Hospital-Acquired (Nosocomial) Infection (HAI).

Hospital-Acquired Infection (HAI / nosocomial infection) is defined as an infection not present or incubating at the time of admission, occurring ≥48 hours after admission, within 30 days of a surgical procedure (or 90 days if an implant is placed), or ≥48 hours after discharge. The CDC/NHSN definitions are used universally.

SSI is the most common HAI in surgical patients (≈30% of all HAIs in surgical wards) and is classified by tissue depth:

  • Superficial incisional SSI — skin & subcutaneous tissue, within 30 days; meets at least one of: purulent drainage, organisms isolated from aseptically obtained culture, ≥1 sign of infection (pain/tenderness, swelling, redness, heat), diagnosis by surgeon.
  • Deep incisional SSI — fascial & muscle layers; within 30 days (or 90 days if implant); purulent drainage from deep incision, spontaneous dehiscence, abscess.
  • Organ/Space SSI — any organ/space opened/manipulated during surgery (peritoneal cavity, joint); within 30/90 days; purulent drainage from drain, abscess on imaging/examination.

  1. Hand hygiene — WHO 5 Moments (before patient contact, before aseptic task, after body fluid exposure, after patient contact, after contact with surroundings).   3. Personal protective equipment (PPE) — gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection, shoe covers as appropriate.
  4.   13. Bundle approach — "care bundles" combine multiple evidence-based interventions (ventilator bundle, central-line bundle, SSI bundle) for synergistic effect.
  14. Healthcare worker vaccination — HBV, influenza, varicella, MMR; sick healthcare workers excluded.

The timing of antibiotic prophylaxis is the most modifiable risk factor for SSI — antibiotic must be in the tissue at the time of incision. Definitions (2 marks)

  • Sterilization — the complete destruction or elimination of all viable forms of microorganisms, including bacteria (vegetative & spores), viruses, fungi, protozoa, and prions (where relevant). An object is either sterile or not; there is no "partially sterile".
  • Disinfection — the elimination of pathogenic microorganisms on inanimate objects, but not necessarily bacterial spores. Reduces microbial load to a level safe for handling or use.
  • Antisepsis — use of chemical agents on living tissue (skin, mucous membranes, wounds) to inhibit or eliminate microorganisms.
  • Differences: sterilization kills spores & all microbes; disinfection does not necessarily kill spores; antisepsis is for living tissue.

Levels of Disinfection (brief)

  • High-level disinfection (HLD) — kills all vegetative organisms, mycobacteria, viruses, fungi, and some spores (with prolonged contact). E.g., 2% glutaraldehyde (20–45 min), 0.55% OPA, 7.5% H₂O₂, peracetic acid 0.2%.
  • Intermediate-level disinfection — kills vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, most viruses & fungi; not spores. E.g., 70% alcohol, 1:50 sodium hypochlorite, iodophors, phenolics.
  • Low-level disinfection — kills vegetative bacteria, enveloped viruses, some fungi; not mycobacteria, spores, or non-enveloped viruses. E.g., quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs).

Various Sterilization Techniques (enumeration) (5 marks)

A. Physical Methods

1. Heat — Moist Heat
  • Autoclave — saturated steam under pressure; 121 °C, 15 psi, 15 min (or 134 °C, 30 psi, 3 min for prions). Most widely used; kills spores.
  • Boiling — 100 °C × 10–30 min; kills vegetative bacteria, viruses, fungi; not spores. Disinfection only.
  • Tyndallisation / fractional sterilisation — 100 °C × 30 min on 3 consecutive days; spores germinate between sessions and are killed on next exposure. Used for heat-labile media (egg, serum, sugar).
  • Pasteurisation — 63 °C × 30 min (holder) or 72 °C × 15 sec (flash/HTST) or 132 °C × 1 sec (UHT). Milk, juices; kills M. tuberculosis, Coxiella burnetii, Salmonella, Brucella.
  • Koch/Arnold steamer — non-pressurised steam at 100 °C.
2. Heat — Dry Heat
  • Hot air oven — 160 °C × 2 h (or 170 °C × 1 h, 180 °C × 30 min). Kills by oxidation. Used for glassware, powders, oils, sharp instruments (no corrosion).
  • Flaming — inoculating loop, forceps, mouth of culture tube.
  • Incineration — soiled disposable material, infected carcasses; final disposal method.
3. Filtration
  • Membrane filters — 0.22 µm pore (bacteria), 0.45 µm (yeasts), 0.025 µm (viruses); for heat-labile fluids (antibiotics, sera, vaccines, toxin, virus culture media).
  • HEPA filters — 0.3 µm; for OT air, biosafety cabinets.
  • Depth filters — Seitz, Berkefeld, Chamberland candles (diatomaceous earth, porcelain).
4. Radiation
  • Ionising radiation — gamma rays (⁶⁰Co, ¹³⁷Cs), beta rays (electron beam). Dose 25 kGy. Cold sterilisation; for plastics, syringes, sutures, catheters, single-use devices, biological indicators.
  • Non-ionising radiation — UV light (260 nm wavelength, maximum microbial kill); for OT air, biosafety cabinets, water. Poor penetration.
5. Other Physical Methods
  • Ultrasonic cleaners — cavitation; cleaning not sterilisation.
  • Pulsed light — high-intensity broad-spectrum pulses.

Autoclave — Detailed Description (6 marks)

Principle

When water is heated in a closed vessel under pressure, its boiling point rises above 100 °C. Saturated steam under pressure carries more thermal energy than dry heat or boiling water at the same temperature. The steam condenses on the cooler surface of the load, releasing the latent heat of vaporisation (~2260 kJ/kg), rapidly transferring energy to the surface and raising its temperature. The combination of moist heat & pressure rapidly denatures microbial proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids — including the keratin-like coat of bacterial spores. Air is the enemy of steam sterilisation — air pockets act as insulators and lower the temperature in those spots; hence efficient air removal is essential.

  1. Pressure vessel (chamber) — stainless steel, withstands 30 psi or more; jacketed (steam circulates in jacket to maintain temperature).
  2. Door — locking mechanism (single or double door for pass-through), safety interlock prevents opening under pressure.
  3. Steam generator — internal or external; supplies saturated steam.
  4. Vacuum pump — in pre-vacuum (porous load) autoclaves; removes air before steam entry.
  5. Pressure & temperature gauges — front panel display & printed chart.
  6. Safety valve — mechanical pressure relief.
  7. Drain / condensate trap — removes condensed water.
  8. Exhaust valve — releases steam at end of cycle.
  9. Recorder / printer — permanent cycle record (temperature-time-pressure graph).

  1. Gravity displacement autoclave — steam enters top, pushes heavier air downward through drain; cheapest; air removal incomplete (≈70%). Used for unwrapped instruments, fluids, laboratory media.
  2. Pre-vacuum (porous load) autoclave — vacuum pump removes air to negative pressure before steam entry (multiple pulses); best for wrapped, porous loads (linen, packs, surgical sets); achieves uniform steam penetration.
  3. Steam-flush pressure-pulse — alternating steam flushes & pressure pulses remove air; no vacuum pump required.

Procedure

  1. Load the chamber — packages loosely arranged, on racks; standing upright if possible; do not stack tightly; place chemical indicator inside each pack.
  2. Place biological indicator (e.g., G. stearothermophilus spore strip) in the most difficult-to-sterilise location (centre of densest pack, bottom of chamber).
  3. Close & lock the door.
  4. Select cycle (gravity / pre-vacuum; 121 °C/15 min, 134 °C/3 min, etc.).
  5. Start cycle — air removal (gravity or vacuum); steam admission to chamber until pressure reaches 15 psi & temperature 121 °C.
  6. Holding phase — 15 min at 121 °C (starts when load reaches 121 °C, not chamber).
  7. Depressurisation — steam exhausted slowly (to prevent boiling of liquids — "flash boiling"); vacuum-assisted drying for wrapped items (10–20 min).
  8. Door opens automatically when safe; unload only when load is dry & cool.
  9. Record cycle parameters; store sterile packs in clean, dry, closed cupboard; use within 30 days (paper wrap) or 180 days (crepe paper / heat-seal pouch).

  • Surgical instruments, dental instruments, vaginal specula, ophthalmic instruments (short cycle for sharp edges).
  • Linen, gowns, drapes, gloves (reusable).
  • Microbiological culture media — nutrient agar, blood agar base, Robertson's cooked meat, fluid thioglycollate (sugar media on short cycle).
  • Glassware, laboratory plastics (polypropylene, PMP, PTFE, silicone).
  • Aqueous solutions — saline, distilled water, buffers.
  • Biohazardous waste — used cultures, swabs, contaminated material before disposal.
  • Soiled linen from infectious patients.
  • Items that cannot be autoclaved: heat-labile plastics (PE, PS, PET), oils, greases, powders, sharp instruments that may corrode (use dry heat or EtO), electronics, optical instruments (endoscopes — use HLD), thermolabile drugs.

Sterilization Control (2 marks)

  1. Physical indicators — pressure gauge, temperature gauge, cycle timer, printed graph of temperature vs time; door interlock.
  2. Chemical indicators
    • Autoclave tape (external) — diagonal stripes change colour when exposed to 121 °C (cream→black). Confirms processing only.
    • Bowie-Dick test — daily test of pre-vacuum autoclave air removal; uniform colour change of indicator sheet = pass; spots = air pockets → pump fault.
    • Class 1–6 chemical indicators (multi-parameter strips placed inside pack) — respond to temperature, time, steam; Class 6 = emulating indicator (equivalent to biological).
  3. Biological indicators (gold standard) — spores of Geobacillus stearothermophilus (10⁶ spores) in a self-contained ampoule; incubated at 55–60 °C for 24–48 h (1–3 h with rapid readout — fluorescent enzyme). No growth = pass. Run weekly & for every load containing implants. For dry heat oven, Bacillus atrophaeus spores; for EtO, B. atrophaeus; for radiation, B. pumilus.

The autoclave is the workhorse of any CSSD (Central Sterile Services Department) — but it is only as good as its loading technique. A common error is to place wrapped packs flat & stacked tightly, which prevents steam penetration to the centre; packs should be placed on edge with 2.5 cm gaps. Liquids should never fill <75% of the flask (to allow for boiling) and the cycle should use slow exhaust to prevent boil-over. For prion disease (CJD/vCJD), the WHO recommends 1N NaOH soak for 1 hour → autoclave at 134 °C × 18 min (single vacuum) or 134 °C × 3 min × 6 cycles; even this may not be fully effective, so single-use instruments are preferred for known CJD patients. The Bowie-Dick test should be done every morning before the first load to confirm vacuum pump efficiency — a single failed test means the entire day's loads are suspect until repaired.

Memory B & T cells persist for decades (some lifelong) — higher frequency than naïve cells, lower activation threshold, more rapid effector function. The clinical picture — abrupt onset of profuse painless watery (rice-water) diarrhoea & vomiting, with no fever, leading to rapid dehydration; stool showing darting motile bacteria (direct wet mount); clustering of cases (family & locality) — is classic for Cholera.

Biotypes: Classical (less virulent, caused 6th pandemic), El Tor (7th pandemic, 1961–present; haemagglutinates chicken RBCs, resistant to polymyxin B 50 U, Voges-Proskauer positive), Haiti variant (hybrid). O139 Bengal emerged in 1992 in Chennai; capsule-positive; may replace O1 in future epidemics.

(B) Pathogenicity of Vibrio cholerae (5 marks)

Source & Transmission

  • Reservoir — humans (cases & asymptomatic carriers); aquatic environment (brackish water, estuaries — copepods, zooplankton, crustaceans, shellfish where vibrios attach to chitin).
  • Transmission — faecal-oral route via contaminated water (primary); contaminated food (seafood — oysters; contaminated rice, millet); person-to-person less common due to high infectious dose.

  • Incubation period — 2 hours to 5 days (usually 1–3 days).

Pathogenesis — Step by Step

  1. Entry & survival through stomach — vibrios are acid-sensitive; high inoculum required to survive gastric acid; reach small intestine alkaline environment where they thrive (pH 8–9 optimum).
  2. Colonisation of small intestine — vibrios do NOT invade the mucosa. They attach to the brush border of mature enterocytes in the jejunum & ileum via:
    • Flagellum — darting motility (chemotaxis toward mucus); seen on direct wet mount — characteristic "shooting star" movement, inhibited by adding anti-cholera serum (immobilisation test).
    • Mucinase — digests mucus to reach epithelium.
    • TCP (toxin-coregulated pilus) — type IV bundle-forming pilus; essential receptor for CTXφ bacteriophage that carries the cholera toxin gene; critical colonisation factor; protective antigen (basis of live oral vaccine CVD 103-HgR).
    • Accessory colonisation factors (ACF) — coregulated with TCP & CT.
    • Haemagglutinin/protease — breaks down mucin, fibronectin, lactoferrin; aids detachment & shedding.
  3. Cholera Toxin (CT) production — the principal virulence factor, encoded by ctxAB gene carried on the genome of CTXφ (lysogenic filamentous bacteriophage); only vibrios lysogenised by CTXφ produce toxin.
    • Structure — AB₅ enterotoxin; 84 kDa. A subunit (28 kDa) = active enzymatic moiety; B subunit (5 × 11.6 kDa) = binding pentamer that binds GM1 ganglioside on enterocyte brush border.

Vibrios remain in the lumen; they do NOT invade the mucosa, cause inflammation, or produce blood/pus in stool. The cholera stool — "rice-water" — is pathognomonic: clear fluid flecked with mucus, like water in which rice has been washed. (A) Type of Hypersensitivity Reaction (1 mark)

The patient's symptoms — intensely itchy, raised, erythematous wheals appearing within 2 hours of peanut ingestion, with a similar prior episode — are the classic presentation of acute urticaria due to Type I (immediate / IgE-mediated / anaphylactic) hypersensitivity to peanut allergen.

Peanut allergy is one of the most common causes of food-induced anaphylaxis. The onset within minutes to 2 hours, recurrence on re-exposure, wheal-and-flare morphology, and intense pruritus are hallmarks of IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the dermis.

(B) Mechanism in Detail (8 marks)

Phase 1 — Sensitisation (First Exposure)

  1. Allergen entry — peanut allergens (Ara h 1, Ara h 2, Ara h 3, Ara h 6 — seed storage proteins; glycoproteins resistant to heat & digestion) are absorbed across the gastrointestinal mucosa. Ara h 2 and Ara h 6 are the most potent allergens (2S albumins).
  2. Antigen uptake — gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) dendritic cells / Peyer's patch M cells capture allergen; process & present peptide on MHC-II to naïve CD4+ T cells in mesenteric lymph nodes.
  3. Th2 polarisation — in atopic individuals, naïve CD4+ T cells differentiate into Th2 cells (rather than Th1 or Treg). Promoted by:
    • Genetic predisposition — atopy locus 5q (IL-4, IL-13, IL-9 cluster), 11q (FcεRIβ), 16p (IL-4Rα).
    • Hygiene hypothesis — reduced microbial exposure in early life (and reduced endotoxin) fails to drive Th1/Treg responses, biasing toward Th2.
    • Epithelium-derived cytokines — TSLP, IL-25, IL-33 — released from damaged barrier (e.g., infantile eczema) → drive DCs to promote Th2.
  4. Th2 cytokine cascade — Th2 cells secrete:
    • IL-4 — B cell class switching to IgE (via STAT6); mast cell growth.
    • IL-13 — IgE class switching, goblet cell hyperplasia, mucus.
    • IL-5 — eosinophil production, activation, survival.
    • IL-9 — mast cell proliferation.
  5. IgE production & sensitisation — plasma cells (in bone marrow, mucosa) secrete allergen-specific IgE. IgE binds with high affinity (Kd 10⁻¹⁰ M) to FcεRI receptors on tissue mast cells (especially skin, GI, respiratory) and circulating basophils. The host is now "sensitised" — asymptomatic but primed.

Phase 2 — Effector Phase (Re-exposure)

  1. Allergen cross-linking — re-exposure to peanut allergen → allergen binds & cross-links two adjacent IgE molecules (each Fab binds one epitope of Ara h 2 etc.) on the mast cell surface → cross-links the underlying FcεRI.
  2. Signal transduction
    • FcεRI is composed of α chain (binds IgE), β chain (amplifier), and 2 γ chains (signalling). Cross-linking phosphorylates ITAMs of β and γ by Lyn (Src family kinase).
    • Syk kinase recruited → activates PLCγ → hydrolyses PIP₂ → IP₃ + DAG.
    • IP₃ → Ca²⁺ release from ER → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺.
    • DAG + Ca²⁺ → activates PKC.
    • Ca²⁺ + calmodulin → calcineurin → NFAT → cytokine transcription.
    • MAPK pathway (Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK) → phospholipase A₂ → arachidonic acid release.

    • Preformed (primary) mediators — released from cytoplasmic granules within 30–60 seconds:
      • Histamine — H1 receptor → vasodilation (nitric oxide), ↑vascular permeability (endothelial contraction → gaps), bronchoconstriction (smooth muscle), sensory nerve stimulation (itch, pain), mucus secretion; H2 receptor → gastric acid, cardiac stimulation.

      • Tryptase, chymase — proteases; activate complement, kinins, PAR-2; tissue remodelling.
      • Eosinophil chemotactic factor-A (ECF-A) — attracts eosinophils.
      • Neutrophil chemotactic factor (NCF-A) — attracts neutrophils.
    • Lipid-derived (secondary) mediators — generated within minutes from arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A₂:
      • Prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) — via COX-1/2 — vasodilation, bronchoconstriction (more potent than histamine), ↑mucus, platelet aggregation, vasodilation (causes erythema/wheal).

      • IL-4, IL-13 — amplify Th2 & IgE class switching (positive feedback); induce VCAM-1 on endothelium → eosinophil recruitment.
      • IL-5 — eosinophil production, activation, survival.

      • GM-CSF — leucocyte production.
      • Stem cell factor (SCF) — mast cell survival & proliferation.

Phase 3 — Late-Phase Reaction (4–8 hours)

Cytokines & lipid mediators recruit eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, and Th2 cells to the skin → sustained inflammation, larger wheals, more intense pruritus. Eosinophils release MBP, ECP, EPO → further tissue damage and itch. Late-phase reaction typically resolves within 24 hours but can persist for days in chronic urticaria. If allergen dose is large or route is parenteral (e.g., IV contrast, insect sting), mast cell degranulation is systemic → widespread vasodilation → distributive shock, increased vascular permeability → angioedema (laryngeal — airway obstruction), bronchospasm (severe), GI smooth muscle spasm (cramping, vomiting, diarrhoea), uterine contraction.   • Non-specific; supports diagnosis of atopy (typically >100 kU/L in atopic individuals) but does not confirm peanut allergy.

  • Basophil activation test (BAT) — flow cytometry measuring CD63/CD203c upregulation on basophils after peanut exposure; high specificity (~95%); functional test (avoids need for oral challenge).

When water is boiled in a closed vessel under increased pressure, its boiling point rises above 100 °C. (B) Life Cycle of Plasmodium (7 marks)

The life cycle involves two hosts: female Anopheles mosquito (definitive host — sexual reproduction) and human (intermediate host — asexual reproduction).

  1. Sporozoite inoculation — infected female Anopheles mosquito (taking a blood meal for egg development) injects sporozoites from her salivary glands into human subcutaneous tissue along with anticoagulant saliva. Sporozoites are spindle-shaped, 10–15 µm, motile.

    • Invade hepatocytes (via sporozoite thrombospondin-related anonymous protein — TRAP & circumsporozoite protein — CSP binding heparan sulfate proteoglycans on hepatocytes).
    • Inside hepatocyte, sporozoite transforms into trophyte → schizont — asexual multiplication produces thousands of merozoites (10,000–30,000 per infected hepatocyte).
    • Hepatocyte ruptures, releasing merozoites into bloodstream.

    • P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. knowlesi — NO hypnozoite stage; no relapse (recrudescence only).

  1. Merozoite invasion — free merozoites invade RBCs via receptor-ligand interaction. P. vivax binds Duffy blood group antigen (Fyᵃ/Fyᵇ) — Duffy-negative individuals (West African population) are resistant. WHO Criteria for Severe Falciparum Malaria

  • Cerebral malaria — impaired consciousness (GCS <11), seizures, coma (Blantyre coma scale <3 in children).
  • Severe anaemia — Hb <7 g/dL (children), <5 g/dL (adults); PCV <20% with parasitaemia >10000/µL.
  • Acute kidney injury — urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h, creatinine >3 mg/dL, urea >20 mmol/L.
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) — pulmonary oedema, hypoxaemia.
  • Hypoglycaemia — blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL).
  • Circulatory collapse / shock — systolic BP <70 mmHg (adults) or <50 mmHg (children).
  • Abnormal bleeding / DIC — spontaneous bleeding from gums, nose, GIT; petechiae.
  • Repeated generalised convulsions — ≥2 in 24 h.
  • Haemoglobinuria — blackwater fever (massive intravascular haemolysis — classically with quinine).
  • Jaundice — bilirubin >3 mg/dL with parasitaemia >100000/µL.
  • Hyperparasitaemia — >2% (low-transmission area) or >10% (high-transmission area) parasitised RBCs; >100,000/µL.
  • Hyperpyrexia — >40 °C.
  • Metabolic acidosis — bicarbonate <15 mmol/L, lactate >5 mmol/L.

Treatment of Severe Falciparum Malaria

  • IV Artesunate — 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 h, then daily until oral tolerated (WHO first-line; ACT after IV course). Reduces mortality by 35% vs quinine (SEAQUAMAT trial).
  • Alternative — IV quinine dihydrochloride 20 mg/kg loading, then 10 mg/kg 8-hourly (ECG monitoring for QT prolongation & hypoglycaemia).
  • After IV therapy — full course of ACT (artemisinin-based combination therapy) — e.g., artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, or artemether-lumefantrine, or artesunate-amodiaquine, or artesunate-mefloquine.
  • Single low-dose primaquine (0.25 mg/kg) — gametocytocidal for falciparum transmission blocking.
  • Supportive — fluids (carefully — avoid fluid overload → pulmonary oedema), correct hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose), blood transfusion if Hb <5 g/dL, haemodialysis if AKI, anticonvulsants (diazepam/phenytoin), broad-spectrum antibiotics if concomitant sepsis.
  • Do NOT use steroids — worsen outcome in cerebral malaria.

Clinical Pearl

In a febrile child from a malaria-endemic region with altered sensorium, the immediate priorities are: (1) confirm parasitaemia by smear or RDT within 1 hour; (2) check blood glucose — hypoglycaemia is a leading cause of death and mimics cerebral malaria; (3) start IV artesunate within 4 hours of suspected severe malaria — do NOT wait for smear confirmation if clinical suspicion is high. IV artesunate reduced mortality by ~35% versus quinine in the landmark SEAQUAMAT trial — and is simpler to administer (no cardiac monitoring, no infusion pump, no hypoglycaemia). Post-artemisinin delayed haemolysis (PADH) — a unique adverse effect occurring 1–3 weeks after IV artesunate — requires Hb monitoring for 4 weeks post-treatment. Always test for G6PD deficiency before giving primaquine (in vivax/ovale radical cure or falciparum gametocytocidal dose) — G6PD-deficient patients develop severe haemolysis. P. knowlesi (SE Asian simian malaria) is the only human malaria with a 24-hour cycle — it can rapidly progress to severe disease; high index of suspicion is needed in patients returning from forested regions of Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines.
